markdownRemark.html:
My legal name is Puanena.

I’ve heard a lot of people look at that name and immediately think, “that must be a girl’s name.” Honestly, I get it.

Even when I was growing up, it already felt like one of those names that people would hear and make a guess right away. And most of the time, the guess was wrong.

Growing up, I dealt with the same awkward moment again and again:

  • people reading my name and assuming I was female
  • people calling me “she” before even meeting me
  • people reaching out to me with the wrong expectation
  • even a few people trying to flirt with me because they thought I was a girl

It sounds funny now, but back then it was kind of annoying and exhausting.

I didn’t choose the name myself. My parents gave it to me before I was born, and sometimes I joked that maybe they wanted a girl more than a boy. I’m not saying that’s actually what they meant — it’s just how it looked from my side sometimes.

When people keep misreading you, it starts to stick.

That’s part of why I started using Ryan as my preferred name.

Ryan feels clearer. Ryan feels more natural in professional settings. Ryan feels like the version of me I want to introduce first.

For a while, I thought this was just a childhood story — one of those funny little things you laugh about later. But as I got older, I realized it wasn’t only a childhood issue.

It followed me into work.

These days, the challenge feels even bigger because first impressions happen fast. Hiring managers skim resumes, scan names, make assumptions, and build a picture of you before you say a single word. And when your name doesn’t match the story people expect, things can get messy fast.

I’ve seen that happen in interviews too many times.

Sometimes the confusion is harmless. Sometimes it’s just awkward. But sometimes it becomes a real problem, because now I’m not only trying to prove my skills — I’m also trying to correct the picture someone built in their head before meeting me.

That extra layer of explanation is tiring. It feels unfair. And honestly, it distracts from what actually matters: my work, my character, and the value I bring.

What I’ve learned is this:

  • names carry identity, history, and family meaning
  • but names also live in the real world, where people make fast assumptions
  • sometimes you have to choose the version of your name that helps you move through the world with less friction

That’s not me rejecting my legal name. It’s me choosing clarity. It’s me protecting my energy. It’s me giving myself room to be seen correctly sooner.

So if you meet me professionally, you’ll probably know me as Ryan. That’s the name I use when I want the conversation to start with who I am, not with a misunderstanding.

And maybe that’s the bigger lesson in all of this:

You don’t have to let other people define the first version of your story.

You can decide how you want to show up. You can choose the name that makes the path a little easier. You can keep the meaning that matters to your family, while still making space for the identity that fits your life now.

For me, that balance is Ryan.

frontmatter.title: Why I Go by Ryan
frontmatter.description: A casual personal story about my name, mistaken identity, and why I go by Ryan
